subject: spatio-temporal variation of environmental covariates and population dynamics

messages.author: c5e00983a5dc591e
messages.subject: spatio-temporal variation of environmental covariates and population dynamics
parts:
Hi everyone, 

I have a general question regarding how best to parameterise a multi-season occupancy model. 

The objective of the model is to assess the relative importance of changing climate and habitat amount on extinction and colonization rates of a bird species over a 20-year period, while accounting for detection probabilities. At each site, and for each year of detection data, I have covariates describing amount of habitat and a heat stress index (yearlySiteCovs). These covariates are both space and time-varying. We also included time-dependence in the extinction component by including 'year' as a factor to examine whether there was a trend over time. In the final model, considering only extinction probabilities for illustrative purposes, this resulted in a single beta estimate for each covariate of habitat and heat stress, and a year factor for each of the 20 years.

I found this post, and am now concerned that including time (here 'year' as a factor) and time-varying covariates may be problematic:
http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=1&t=2363&p=7377&hilit=+temporal+variation+#p7377

My specific questions include:
1) Is it a problem to include both time-varying covariates and time (i.e. 'year') as a factor ? As per the phidot post, the answer to this seems like a 'yes'....and this can result in over-fitting. I would really like to better understand why this is case.

2) For a multi-season occupancy model that includes time-varying covariates, is it possible to get at the variation explained due to temporal vs spatial changes in covariates, and what is the best way to parameterise the model to identify these sources of variation? In a single year model, a covariate describing, for example, % habitat amount for each primary sampled site, and the resulting beta estimates would to my understanding be addressing spatial variation across the sampled sites. In a multi-season occupancy model which includes time-varying covariates on the extinction and colonization terms, do these beta estimates represent spatial or temporal variation? If I included a year as a factor on both extintion/colonization terms, would there be no temporal variation left to be explained by the time-varying covariates of habitat and climate?  I might be missing something obvious here, but any ideas, resources, etc, much appreciated.

I have been working with the R package unmarked, so am posting it here, but happy to send over to another list-serve. Huge thanks to everyone. 

Ilona

messages.author: 0227543d81e2924c
messages.subject: Re: spatio-temporal variation of environmental covariates and population dynamics
parts:
My specific questions include:
1) Is it a problem to include both time-varying covariates and time (i.e. 'year') as a factor ? As per the phidot post, the answer to this seems like a 'yes'....and this can result in over-fitting. I would really like to better understand why this is case.

Simple - The fully time-specific model (t) explains (or, more correctly, structurally specifies)  ALL the variation in the parameter, so that there’s nothing left to be explained by the covariate. 

One of the posts in that thread (made by Jeff Laake) is worth repeating:

"I assume you mean something like

~time + Effort

where Effort has a numeric value for each time and time is a factor variable. Answer is no! It is over-parameterized. 

<insert -- again, if you include time as a factor, then you can't include a temporally varying covariate in the same model. But, as jeff elaborates...>

Now if the formula is for a secondary occasion in a robust design (as often shows up in dynamic occupancy models, for example) and it is something like

~session + Effort 

and Effort varies within secondary occasion that would be perfectly acceptable because there is variation in effort across secondary occasions. ~session would be the intercept for the session and the values for a secondary occasion would be intercept + b*effort_j where effort_j is the effort on the jth secondary occasion. You could even have ~session*Effort - a different intercept and slope for the session..."

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] spatio-temporal variation of environmental covariates and population dynamics
parts:
Hi Ilona,

re. your 2nd question I would go Bayesian and treat annual variation in colonisation or extinction as a random effect. Then, you can treat the proportional reduction in the variance of these effects, when you introduce a covariate, as "proportion of variance explained". Easy in BUGS, but can't be done in unmarked.

Kind regards  ---  Marc

messages.author: d3fd439c2e48caf1
messages.subject: Re: spatio-temporal variation of environmental covariates and population dynamics
parts:
Hi Ilona,

There is a general issue that I think you hit on; without some decomposing of covariates, parameters for a spatiotemporally-varying covariate (say, precipitation) could (depending on how long and over how large an area is studied) be influenced heavily by one "dimension" and only slightly by the other; but we wouldn't know without further digging (despite the certainty I've sometimes seen in discussion sections =) ).

Without additional detail, it's hard to say if including factor(year) would be over-fitting in your model. If most of the variation is over time (for example, temperature in a small study area), then yes. If spread over space and time, then inclusion of factor(year) would result in a parameter estimate (say, for % habitat) that is addressing the spatial variation (some good simulations showing this in a different context: van de Pol, M., and J. Wright. 2009. Animal Behaviour 77:753-758).

To digress a bit, and sticking with the precipitation example, the balance of the variation is over space in a large area like the western U.S., and there's an argument (in this case) for using site-specific means to address the spatial variation in this covariate and anomalies to address temporal variation. BTW, this is standard stuff among climatologists, less so among ecologists! =) In this example (from my experience), other covariates *may* become redundant; for example elevation (cor with precip means) and factor(year) (cor with anomalies).

- G

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: spatio-temporal variation of environmental covariates and population dynamics
parts:
Giancarlo, when you say spatial means vs. temporal anomalies, it sounds like the effects in one dimension (space) are treated as fixed while variation in the other dimension (time) is treated as random.  It seems with enough replication you could specify variation as random in both dimensions, and then the distinction is not necessary.  But maybe climatologists are typically working with data that are far more replicated in time than in space.

I think you make an excellent point that just because variation in a dimension is possible and was recorded, does not mean the model will be able to fit such complexity.  And the variation can be very unbalanced, depending on the scales at each dimension, affecting your ability to make certain inferences.  If you take BBS data for instance, depending on your sample frame there is often more spatial variation in species counts than temporal variation.  This limits the complexity of temporal relationships that can be modeled, unless there is enough spatio-temporal variation.
